Statistics for Non-Detects

Prof. Marc Los Huertos  •  Pomona College

← Back to RTricks

The Problem What It Looks Like The Iceberg Distributions Fail Core Concepts Data Setup Naïve Approaches Kaplan-Meier ROS MLE Method Comparison Hypothesis Tests Reporting

What this module covers. Your water sample contains lead — but the instrument reports “< 0.5 µg/L.” Your air quality sensor flags a PM2.5 reading as below detection. Your lab report records E. coli as “absent.” These non-detects (also called left-censored observations) are one of the most common data problems in environmental science, and naïve approaches — substituting zero, or half the detection limit — introduce systematic bias. We open with four diagnostic graphics that show exactly how and why standard distributional tools fail on censored data. Then we teach four principled methods: the Kaplan–Meier estimator, Regression on Order Statistics (ROS), and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). Datasets drawn from water quality (E. coli, phosphorus, lead) and air quality (PM2.5) show where each method shines.

1. The Non-Detect Problem

Instruments have physical limits. An ICP-MS spectrometer measuring dissolved lead in drinking water cannot reliably distinguish a concentration of 0.05 µg/L from 0.00 µg/L; below some threshold — the method detection limit (MDL) or reporting limit (RL) — the measurement is replaced by a flag: <MDL. An air quality monitor logs PM2.5 as zero on days when actual concentrations are near zero but indistinguishable from instrument noise.

These flagged values are not zero. The true concentration lies somewhere in the interval [0, MDL]. Treating them as zero, as missing data, or using simple substitution rules creates systematic bias that corrupts means, standard deviations, percentile estimates, trend tests, and group comparisons. The rest of this module explains why — starting with a concrete picture of what censored data actually looks like.

🔑 Non-detects = left-censored observations

A non-detect at reporting limit L means: “the true value is somewhere in [0, L].” The observation is not missing — it is censored. This is the mirror image of right-censoring in survival analysis (Module 12), where we know an event had not yet occurred by time t. Here we know a concentration is below threshold L. The statistical machinery is identical; only the direction of censoring flips.

1.1 What censored data look like in the field

The code below builds a small phosphorus dataset (the same structure used throughout this module) so we can visualise the problem before any analysis. The “observed” column is what your spreadsheet contains after the lab delivers results: detected values plus zeros where the instrument flagged < RL.

set.seed(42)
# Simulate 40 true log-normal TP values; RL = 5 µg/L
n_prev  <- 40
rl_prev <- 5
true_preview <- rlnorm(n_prev, meanlog = 2.0, sdlog = 0.9)
obs_preview  <- ifelse(true_preview >= rl_prev, true_preview, 0)
cen_preview  <- true_preview < rl_prev

preview_df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = 1:n_prev,
  true      = round(true_preview, 2),
  observed  = round(obs_preview,  2),
  censored  = cen_preview,
  rl        = rl_prev
)

# What the analyst actually sees (no "true" column in real life)
head(preview_df[, c("sample_id", "observed", "censored", "rl")], 12)
##    sample_id observed censored rl
## 1          1    25.38    FALSE  5
## 2          2     0.00     TRUE  5
## 3          3    10.25    FALSE  5
## 4          4    13.06    FALSE  5
## 5          5    10.63    FALSE  5
## 6          6     6.72    FALSE  5
## 7          7    28.80    FALSE  5
## 8          8     6.79    FALSE  5
## 9          9    45.45    FALSE  5
## 10        10     6.98    FALSE  5
## 11        11    23.91    FALSE  5
## 12        12    57.86    FALSE  5
knitr::opts_current$set(fig.cap = "What the analyst sees (top strip) vs. the true concentrations (bottom strip) for 40 simulated phosphorus samples. Detected values (filled circles) are identical in both panels. Non-detects (open triangles) appear at zero in the analyst's data but are scattered across [0, RL] in truth. The grey shaded band marks the unobservable region below the reporting limit.")
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

cols_nd  <- "#c62828"   # non-detect colour
cols_det <- "#2d5a3d"   # detected colour

make_strip <- function(df, y_col, title_txt) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = sample_id, y = .data[[y_col]])) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = rl_prev,
             fill = "#f0f0f0", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = rl_prev, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "#888", linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = subset(df, !censored),
               colour = cols_det, size = 2.2, shape = 19) +
    geom_point(data = subset(df, censored),
               colour = cols_nd,  size = 2.8, shape = 25,
               fill = cols_nd, alpha = 0.7) +
    annotate("text", x = n_prev - 1, y = rl_prev + 0.8,
             label = paste0("RL = ", rl_prev, " µg/L"),
             colour = "#666", size = 3.2, hjust = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, max(true_preview) * 1.05)) +
    labs(x = "Sample ID", y = "TP (µg/L)", title = title_txt) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(family = "serif", face = "bold",
                                    colour = "#1e3a2f", size = 11),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

p_analyst <- make_strip(preview_df, "observed",
                         "What the analyst sees  (non-detects coded as 0)")
p_truth   <- make_strip(preview_df, "true",
                         "The truth  (non-detects scattered in [0, RL])")

(p_analyst / p_truth) +
  plot_annotation(
    caption = "Filled circles = detected values  |  Red triangles = non-detects  |  Grey band = unobservable region"
  )

The key insight from these two panels: the analyst’s dataset and the true dataset are identical above the RL. Every difference lies in that grey band. The analyst knows something is there — just not how much. Statistical methods that ignore or misrepresent that grey band will produce biased summaries.

1.2 The iceberg: how much information is hidden?

Think of a non-detect dataset as an iceberg. The detected values are the visible tip; the non-detects are the submerged mass. How much of the distribution sits below the waterline depends on where the RL falls relative to the distribution’s centre.

knitr::opts_current$set(fig.cap = "The 'iceberg' of a log-normal distribution truncated at a reporting limit. The solid green curve is the true log-normal PDF; the filled (teal) area is what the analyst observes above the RL; the hatched (grey) area is the censored region that conventional analysis discards or misrepresents. Three different RLs are shown to illustrate how censoring fraction changes. When RL sits near the median, nearly half the distribution is invisible.")
par(mar = c(4.5, 4, 3.5, 1.5), las = 1)

mu_ice <- 2.0; sd_ice <- 0.85   # log-normal parameters
x_seq  <- seq(0.01, 60, length.out = 500)
y_dens <- dlnorm(x_seq, meanlog = mu_ice, sdlog = sd_ice)

rls    <- c(2, 5, 12)
cols_rl <- c("#4a7c5e", "#c8832a", "#c62828")
labels  <- c("RL = 2  (10% censored)", "RL = 5  (35% censored)",
             "RL = 12  (65% censored)")

plot(x_seq, y_dens, type = "n",
     xlab = "Concentration (µg/L)", ylab = "Probability density",
     main = "How much of the distribution is hidden by the reporting limit?",
     ylim = c(0, max(y_dens) * 1.12), cex.main = 0.93)

# Fill detected region (above highest RL) to show "observable" area
x_above <- x_seq[x_seq >= max(rls)]
polygon(c(max(rls), x_above, max(x_seq)),
        c(0, dlnorm(x_above, mu_ice, sd_ice), 0),
        col = adjustcolor("#d4e6da", 0.9), border = NA)

# True distribution
lines(x_seq, y_dens, col = "#1e3a2f", lwd = 2.5)

# Shade censored regions and draw RL lines
for (k in seq_along(rls)) {
  rl_k  <- rls[k]
  x_cen <- x_seq[x_seq <= rl_k]
  pct   <- round(plnorm(rl_k, mu_ice, sd_ice) * 100)
  polygon(c(0, x_cen, rl_k),
          c(0, dlnorm(x_cen, mu_ice, sd_ice), 0),
          col  = adjustcolor(cols_rl[k], 0.22),
          border = NA)
  abline(v = rl_k, col = cols_rl[k], lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
  text(rl_k + 0.5, max(y_dens) * (0.95 - (k - 1) * 0.14),
       labels[k], col = cols_rl[k], adj = 0, cex = 0.78)
}

legend("topright",
       legend = c("True distribution", "Observable region (above max RL)"),
       col    = c("#1e3a2f", adjustcolor("#d4e6da", 0.9)),
       lty    = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 15), pt.cex = 2,
       lwd    = c(2.5, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.82)

When the RL is modest relative to the distribution (10% censoring), naïve substitution is forgivable. When it sits near the median (50%+ censoring), you are trying to describe a mountain while only seeing the upper half. No substitution rule can recover that information; only principled censored-data methods can.

1.3 How standard distributional tools fail

When analysts ignore censoring and treat the non-detects as zeros (or drop them), three classes of diagnostic plot all give misleading pictures. The figure below shows the same 40-sample TP dataset analysed four ways, side-by-side with the ground truth.

knitr::opts_current$set(fig.cap = "Four distributional diagnostics applied to the same phosphorus dataset under three data-handling strategies: the true (uncensored) values, naive zero-substitution, and the principled ROS-imputed complete dataset. Top row: histograms on the raw scale. Middle row: kernel density on the log scale (where log-normal data should be symmetric and bell-shaped). Bottom row: normal Q-Q plots on the log scale (where a log-normal should follow the diagonal). Zero-substitution breaks the log-scale symmetry, creates a spike at log(0), and produces a severe downward hook in the Q-Q plot - all false artefacts of the data-handling choice, not features of the environment.")
library(NADA)

# Principled comparison dataset (ROS imputation)
ros_prev <- cenros(obs_preview, cen_preview)
imp_vals <- ros_prev$modeled          # full imputed dataset

# Three versions of the data
d_true <- true_preview
d_zero <- obs_preview                 # 0 for NDs
d_ros  <- imp_vals

# Labels
lab3 <- c("True values\n(oracle)", "Naïve: substitute 0", "ROS-imputed\n(principled)")
col3 <- c("#1e3a2f", "#c62828", "#4a7c5e")

par(mfrow = c(3, 3),
    mar   = c(3.8, 3.8, 2.8, 0.8),
    oma   = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
    las   = 1, cex.axis = 0.82, cex.lab = 0.88)

# ── Row 1: Histograms (raw scale) ────────────────────────────────────────────
for (k in 1:3) {
  vals <- list(d_true, d_zero, d_ros)[[k]]
  # Use the full range (including any zeros) so breaks always span the data
  br   <- pretty(vals, n = 12)
  # Ensure the leftmost break is at or below min(vals)
  if (br[1] > min(vals)) br <- c(min(vals), br)
  hist(vals,
       breaks  = br,
       col     = adjustcolor(col3[k], 0.45),
       border  = "white",
       main    = lab3[k],
       xlab    = "TP (µg/L)", ylab = "Count",
       cex.main = 0.88)
  abline(v = rl_prev, lty = 2, col = "#888", lwd = 1.4)
  if (k == 1) mtext("Histogram (raw scale)", side = 2, line = 2.6,
                    cex = 0.78, col = "#555", las = 0)
}

# ── Row 2: KDE on log scale ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
# For zero-substitution, add small offset so log() is defined
log_zero  <- log(pmax(d_zero, 0.05))   # 0 → 0.05 to avoid -Inf
log_true  <- log(d_true)
log_ros   <- log(d_ros)

x_log <- seq(-3, 6, length.out = 300)
dens_list <- list(density(log_true, bw = "SJ"),
                  density(log_zero, bw = "SJ"),
                  density(log_ros,  bw = "SJ"))
y_max <- max(sapply(dens_list, function(d) max(d$y))) * 1.1

for (k in 1:3) {
  d <- dens_list[[k]]
  plot(d, main = "", xlab = "log(TP) [µg/L]", ylab = "Density",
       col = col3[k], lwd = 2.2,
       xlim = c(-3, 6), ylim = c(0, y_max))
  polygon(c(d$x[1], d$x, d$x[length(d$x)]),
          c(0, d$y, 0),
          col = adjustcolor(col3[k], 0.20), border = NA)
  abline(v = log(rl_prev), lty = 2, col = "#888", lwd = 1.4)
  if (k == 2) {
    # Annotate the zero-spike artefact
    x_spike <- log(0.05)
    arrows(x_spike + 0.3, y_max * 0.6, x_spike + 0.05, y_max * 0.35,
           length = 0.08, col = "#c62828", lwd = 1.5)
    text(x_spike + 0.35, y_max * 0.62, "artefact\nspike",
         col = "#c62828", cex = 0.70, adj = 0)
  }
  if (k == 1) mtext("KDE on log scale", side = 2, line = 2.6,
                    cex = 0.78, col = "#555", las = 0)
}

# ── Row 3: Normal Q–Q on log scale ──────────────────────────────────────────
for (k in 1:3) {
  lv <- list(log_true, log_zero, log_ros)[[k]]
  qq <- qqnorm(lv, plot.it = FALSE)
  plot(qq$x, qq$y,
       pch  = 19, cex = 0.85,
       col  = adjustcolor(col3[k], 0.8),
       xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
       ylab = "Sample quantiles",
       main = "")
  qqline(lv, col = "#888", lwd = 1.4, lty = 2)
  if (k == 2) {
    # Annotate the hook
    n_hook <- sum(d_zero == 0)
    y_hook <- sort(log_zero)[n_hook]
    x_hook <- qq$x[order(lv)[n_hook]]
    arrows(x_hook - 0.5, y_hook - 0.3, x_hook - 0.1, y_hook - 0.05,
           length = 0.08, col = "#c62828", lwd = 1.5)
    text(x_hook - 0.55, y_hook - 0.38, "downward\nhook",
         col = "#c62828", cex = 0.70, adj = 1)
  }
  if (k == 1) mtext("Q–Q plot (log scale)", side = 2, line = 2.6,
                    cex = 0.78, col = "#555", las = 0)
}

mtext("How data-handling strategy distorts distributional diagnostics",
      outer = TRUE, cex = 0.92, font = 2, col = "#1e3a2f")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Read each column top-to-bottom. The true values (left column) show a right-skewed histogram, a symmetric bell on the log scale, and a straight Q–Q line — exactly what a log-normal distribution looks like. The naïve zero-substitution column (centre) tells a completely different story: a spike of zeros at the left of the histogram, a distorted bimodal kernel density with an artefactual left lobe, and a severe downward hook in the Q–Q plot. That hook is entirely a product of the data-handling choice — it does not reflect any real feature of the environment. A statistician who saw only this column might wrongly conclude the data are bimodal, or that the log-normal model is inappropriate, or that some kind of mixture distribution is needed. The ROS-imputed column (right) closely recovers the true picture.

⚠️ The Q–Q hook is a diagnostic red flag

If you see a sharp downward hook at the left tail of a Q–Q plot on log-transformed environmental data, check your non-detects first. The hook almost always means zeros (or a clump of identical substituted values like MDL/2) have been included in the log-transformed dataset. It is not a distribution problem — it is a censoring problem masquerading as one.

1.4 How the bias compounds: a numerical experiment

The figure below makes the bias concrete across a range of censoring fractions, using 1,000 simulated datasets at each level.

knitr::opts_current$set(fig.cap = "Bias in the estimated mean as a function of censoring fraction, for three data-handling strategies. Each point is the average of 500 simulated log-normal datasets (n = 50, same parameters throughout); the horizontal dashed line is the true mean. Substituting zero produces severe negative bias that grows linearly with censoring fraction. Substituting RL/2 is better but still biased above 20-30%. ROS (using cenros()) tracks the true mean closely across the full range shown.")
set.seed(999)
n_sim   <- 500    # simulations per censoring level (kept low for knit speed)
n_obs   <- 50
mu_b    <- 2.0; sd_b <- 0.85
true_mn <- exp(mu_b + sd_b^2 / 2)   # log-normal mean

cen_targets <- seq(0.05, 0.70, by = 0.05)

results <- lapply(cen_targets, function(target_cen) {
  # Find RL that produces approximately target censoring fraction
  rl_b <- qlnorm(target_cen, mu_b, sd_b)

  means_zero <- means_half <- means_ros <- numeric(n_sim)
  for (i in seq_len(n_sim)) {
    tv  <- rlnorm(n_obs, mu_b, sd_b)
    cen <- tv < rl_b
    obs <- ifelse(cen, 0, tv)

    means_zero[i] <- mean(obs)
    means_half[i] <- mean(ifelse(cen, rl_b / 2, obs))
    r <- tryCatch(cenros(obs, cen), error = function(e) NULL)
    means_ros[i]  <- if (!is.null(r)) mean(r$modeled) else NA
  }
  data.frame(
    cen_frac  = target_cen,
    bias_zero = mean(means_zero, na.rm = TRUE) - true_mn,
    bias_half = mean(means_half, na.rm = TRUE) - true_mn,
    bias_ros  = mean(means_ros,  na.rm = TRUE) - true_mn
  )
}) |> do.call(rbind, args = _)

par(mar = c(4.5, 5, 3.5, 1.5), las = 1)
plot(results$cen_frac * 100, results$bias_zero,
     type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2,
     col  = "#c62828",
     xlab = "Censoring fraction (%)",
     ylab = "Bias in estimated mean  (estimate - true)",
     main = "Bias in estimated mean vs. censoring fraction",
     ylim = range(c(results$bias_zero, results$bias_half,
                    results$bias_ros), na.rm = TRUE) * c(1.1, 1.3),
     cex.main = 0.93)
lines(results$cen_frac * 100, results$bias_half,
      type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2, col = "#e65100")
lines(results$cen_frac * 100, results$bias_ros,
      type = "b", pch = 15, lwd = 2, col = "#2d5a3d")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "#555", lwd = 1.5)

legend("bottomleft",
       legend = c("Substitute 0", "Substitute RL/2", "ROS (principled)"),
       col    = c("#c62828", "#e65100", "#2d5a3d"),
       pch    = c(19, 17, 15), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.88)

Two take-aways from this simulation. First, substituting zero is never unbiased: even at 5% censoring, the mean is already measurably underestimated. Second, RL/2 substitution is approximately unbiased up to about 15–20% censoring but degrades rapidly beyond that. ROS stays close to the dashed zero-bias line across the full range shown. This is why the EPA, USGS, and Helsel (2012) all recommend moving beyond substitution methods for datasets with more than 15% non-detects.

1.5 The regulatory and scientific context

Environmental agencies routinely encounter datasets with 30–80% non-detects:

  • EPA Method 200.8 for metals in water has MDLs of 0.02–2 µg/L for trace metals; clean background groundwater frequently falls below these limits.
  • E. coli monitoring in recreational waters: when conditions are good, many samples return “below 1 CFU/100 mL.”
  • PM2.5 daily averages near rural background sites can fall below 2–3 µg/m³, the typical FRM instrument noise floor.
  • Total phosphorus in oligotrophic reference lakes: 5–20 µg/L MDLs mean half the spring samples may be non-detects.

Getting the statistics right matters for regulatory compliance (is this site exceeding the 303(d) listing criterion?), trend detection (is lead declining post-ban?), and risk assessment (what is the 95th percentile exposure?).

2. Core Concepts

Detection limit vocabulary

Term Abbreviation Definition
Method Detection Limit MDL Lowest concentration distinguishable from blank at 99% confidence (EPA)
Reporting Limit RL Practical limit used in lab reports; often 3–5 × MDL
Limit of Detection LOD Generic term; use carefully — meaning varies by lab
Limit of Quantitation LOQ Level above which measurement is acceptably precise; typically 3–10 × MDL
Minimum Reporting Level MRL USGS term equivalent to RL

In this tutorial we use reporting limit (RL) as the generic term for the censoring threshold. A measurement reported as < RL is a non-detect.

Left censoring versus right censoring

In survival analysis (right censoring), we observe time up to some cutoff c and know only that T > c. Here, with left censoring, we observe that a concentration C is known only to satisfy C < RL. The Kaplan–Meier estimator handles both through a symmetric reversal: we flip the data, apply the standard KM algorithm, then flip the estimated CDF back.

The fraction censored matters

The appropriate method depends heavily on what fraction of your data is below the reporting limit:

Censoring fraction Recommended approaches
< 15% Any substitution method is likely acceptable; ROS preferred
15–50% ROS or MLE; avoid substitution
50–80% MLE or Kaplan–Meier; be cautious about distributional assumptions
> 80% Kaplan–Meier only; summary statistics become unreliable

⚠️ Multiple detection limits

A single dataset often contains measurements from different laboratories, different years, or different analytical methods — each with its own RL. This is called multiply-censored data. The Kaplan–Meier and ROS methods handle multiple RLs naturally. Simple substitution methods (½ MDL) cannot, because there is no single substitution value to use.

3. Packages and Data Setup

Required packages

# Core statistical methods for non-detects
library(NADA)       # cenros(), cenfit(), cencdf(), cenmle(), and hypothesis tests
library(NADA2)      # updated companion: cenperm2(), cen2means(), cenQQ()
library(survival)   # underlying Surv() infrastructure

# Data wrangling and visualization
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # combine ggplot panels
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

💡 Installing NADA and NADA2

NADA is on CRAN: install.packages("NADA"). NADA2 may require the development version: install.packages("NADA2") or remotes::install_github("SwampThingPaul/NADA2"). Both implement Dennis Helsel’s methods from Statistics for Censored Environmental Data (Helsel 2012), the authoritative reference for this topic.

Dataset 1: E. coli in recreational water (water quality)

We simulate monthly E. coli monitoring at three beach sites over two years. Units are CFU/100 mL. The state recreational water standard is 235 CFU/100 mL (single-sample). The laboratory reporting limit is 1 CFU/100 mL; samples below this are recorded as 0 in the raw data (a common field convention — zero means non-detect, not absence).

set.seed(2024)

# Helper: simulate log-normal samples with left-censoring at RL
sim_censored <- function(n, meanlog, sdlog, rl) {
  true_vals <- rlnorm(n, meanlog = meanlog, sdlog = sdlog)
  detected  <- true_vals >= rl
  # Observed value: true value if detected, 0 if non-detect (field convention)
  obs       <- ifelse(detected, true_vals, 0)
  data.frame(
    true     = true_vals,
    observed = obs,
    censored = !detected,   # TRUE = non-detect
    rl       = rl
  )
}

# Three beach sites with different E. coli levels
set.seed(101)
ecoli <- bind_rows(
  sim_censored(24, meanlog = 3.2, sdlog = 1.1, rl = 1) |> mutate(site = "Beach A"),
  sim_censored(24, meanlog = 2.4, sdlog = 1.3, rl = 1) |> mutate(site = "Beach B"),
  sim_censored(24, meanlog = 4.1, sdlog = 0.9, rl = 1) |> mutate(site = "Beach C")
)

# Summarise censoring fractions
ecoli |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    n_nd       = sum(censored),
    pct_nd     = round(100 * mean(censored), 1),
    min_det    = round(min(observed[!censored]), 1),
    max_det    = round(max(observed[!censored]), 1)
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Site", "n", "Non-detects", "% ND", "Min detected", "Max detected"),
        caption = "E. coli dataset summary (CFU/100 mL; RL = 1 CFU/100 mL)")
E. coli dataset summary (CFU/100 mL; RL = 1 CFU/100 mL)
Site n Non-detects % ND Min detected Max detected
Beach A 24 0 0.0 2.6 118.0
Beach B 24 2 8.3 1.3 51.8
Beach C 24 0 0.0 15.9 259.3

Dataset 2: Total phosphorus in lake monitoring (water quality)

Total phosphorus (TP) in a temperate lake monitored quarterly at surface and deep stations. Units are µg/L. The RL is 5 µg/L; values below this are coded as 0. Elevated TP indicates eutrophication risk.

set.seed(202)
tp <- bind_rows(
  sim_censored(30, meanlog = 2.1, sdlog = 0.8, rl = 5) |> mutate(depth = "Surface"),
  sim_censored(30, meanlog = 2.8, sdlog = 0.7, rl = 5) |> mutate(depth = "Deep")
)

tp |>
  group_by(depth) |>
  summarise(n = n(), n_nd = sum(censored),
            pct_nd = round(100 * mean(censored), 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Depth", "n", "Non-detects", "% ND"),
        caption = "Total phosphorus dataset summary (µg/L; RL = 5 µg/L)")
Total phosphorus dataset summary (µg/L; RL = 5 µg/L)
Depth n Non-detects % ND
Deep 30 1 3.3
Surface 30 7 23.3

Dataset 3: Lead (Pb) in drinking water (water quality)

Lead sampling at 50 household taps under a Tier 2 monitoring plan. Units are µg/L. The EPA action level is 15 µg/L; the RL is 0.5 µg/L. Many modern homes with no lead service lines return non-detects.

set.seed(303)
pb <- sim_censored(50, meanlog = 0.8, sdlog = 1.4, rl = 0.5) |>
  mutate(tap_id = paste0("Tap_", sprintf("%02d", 1:50)))

cat("Lead dataset: n =", nrow(pb),
    " | Non-detects:", sum(pb$censored),
    " (", round(100 * mean(pb$censored), 1), "%)\n")
## Lead dataset: n = 50  | Non-detects: 6  ( 12 %)
cat("Detection range:", round(range(pb$observed[!pb$censored]), 2), "µg/L\n")
## Detection range: 0.56 56.5 µg/L

Dataset 4: PM2.5 daily concentrations (air quality)

Daily PM2.5 at a rural background monitoring site over one year. Units are µg/m³. The RL is 2 µg/m³; days with very clean air register as 0. The 24-hour NAAQS is 35 µg/m³.

set.seed(404)
# PM2.5: slight seasonal signal (higher in winter), mostly below RL in summer
pm25 <- data.frame(
  doy = 1:365
) |>
  mutate(
    # true seasonal log-mean: peaks in winter (day ~15, ~350), dips in summer
    meanlog   = 1.6 + 0.5 * cos(2 * pi * (doy - 15) / 365),
    true_conc = rlnorm(365, meanlog = meanlog, sdlog = 0.9),
    observed  = ifelse(true_conc >= 2, true_conc, 0),
    censored  = true_conc < 2,
    rl        = 2,
    season    = cut(doy, breaks = c(0, 79, 171, 263, 355, 366),
                    labels = c("Winter","Spring","Summer","Fall","Winter2"),
                    include.lowest = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(season = recode(season, "Winter2" = "Winter"))

cat("PM2.5 dataset: n =", nrow(pm25),
    " | Non-detects:", sum(pm25$censored),
    " (", round(100 * mean(pm25$censored), 1), "%)\n")
## PM2.5 dataset: n = 365  | Non-detects: 59  ( 16.2 %)

4. Why Naïve Approaches Fail

Before introducing principled methods, let us see exactly how badly the common shortcuts perform using the lead dataset, where we have the true values available for comparison.

# Compute summary stats under each substitution strategy
sub_zero    <- pb$observed                          # non-detects treated as 0
sub_half    <- ifelse(pb$censored, pb$rl / 2, pb$observed)  # RL/2
sub_rl      <- ifelse(pb$censored, pb$rl,     pb$observed)  # substitute RL
true_vals   <- pb$true

# Use ROS (Section 6) for comparison — computed here, explained later
ros_fit     <- cenros(pb$observed, pb$censored)
sub_ros     <- ros_fit$modeled

methods_df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(value = true_vals,  method = "True values"),
  data.frame(value = sub_zero,   method = "Substitute 0"),
  data.frame(value = sub_half,   method = "Substitute RL/2"),
  data.frame(value = sub_rl,     method = "Substitute RL"),
  data.frame(value = sub_ros,    method = "ROS (principled)")
) |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("True values","Substitute 0",
                                            "Substitute RL/2","Substitute RL",
                                            "ROS (principled)")))

ggplot(methods_df, aes(x = log(value + 0.01), fill = method, colour = method)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.30, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("#1e3a2f","#c62828","#e65100","#c8832a","#2d5a3d")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1e3a2f","#c62828","#e65100","#c8832a","#2d5a3d")) +
  labs(x = "log(Pb concentration, µg/L)", y = "Density",
       title = "Lead (Pb): substitution methods vs. true distribution",
       fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_text(family = "serif", face = "bold", colour = "#1e3a2f"))

Distribution of lead concentrations by substitution method vs. the true distribution. Substituting zero collapses the lower tail entirely; substituting RL/2 is closer but systematically underestimates the lower tail. The ROS method (introduced in Section 6) closely recovers the true distribution. 

bias_table <- data.frame(
  Method   = c("True values", "Substitute 0", "Substitute RL/2",
                "Substitute RL", "ROS (principled)"),
  Mean     = round(c(mean(true_vals), mean(sub_zero), mean(sub_half),
                     mean(sub_rl),    mean(sub_ros)), 3),
  Median   = round(c(median(true_vals), median(sub_zero), median(sub_half),
                     median(sub_rl),    median(sub_ros)), 3),
  SD       = round(c(sd(true_vals), sd(sub_zero), sd(sub_half),
                     sd(sub_rl),    sd(sub_ros)), 3),
  P95      = round(c(quantile(true_vals, 0.95), quantile(sub_zero, 0.95),
                     quantile(sub_half, 0.95),  quantile(sub_rl, 0.95),
                     quantile(sub_ros, 0.95)), 3)
)

kable(bias_table,
      col.names = c("Method", "Mean (µg/L)", "Median (µg/L)", "SD", "95th pct"),
      caption   = "Summary statistics under different non-detect treatments. True values serve as the benchmark. ROS best recovers the true distribution statistics.") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped") |>
  row_spec(1, bold = TRUE, color = "#1e3a2f") |>
  row_spec(5, bold = TRUE, color = "#2d5a3d")
Summary statistics under different non-detect treatments. True values serve as the benchmark. ROS best recovers the true distribution statistics.
Method Mean (µg/L) Median (µg/L) SD 95th pct
True values 5.206 2.413 8.828 17.02
Substitute 0 5.163 2.413 8.853 17.02
Substitute RL/2 5.193 2.413 8.836 17.02
Substitute RL 5.223 2.413 8.819 17.02
ROS (principled) 5.194 2.413 8.835 17.02

⚠️ The substitution bias is systematic, not random

Substituting zero always underestimates the mean and standard deviation. This is not sampling error that averages out — it is structural bias that worsens as the censoring fraction increases. With 40% non-detects, substituting zero can underestimate the true mean by 20–50%.

5. Kaplan–Meier for Left-Censored Data

The Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator is the non-parametric workhorse for censored data. It makes no distributional assumption — it simply estimates the empirical CDF from the data as they are, treating non-detects as left-censored observations.

The flip trick

Standard KM is designed for right-censoring (T > c). To handle left-censoring (C < RL), we flip the data: let x’ = max(x) − x and apply the right-censored KM estimator, then flip the estimated CDF back. The NADA package’s cenfit() does this automatically.

# Kaplan-Meier for E. coli at Beach A
beach_a <- ecoli |> filter(site == "Beach A")

# cenfit(obs, censored_indicator)  — censored = TRUE means non-detect
km_a <- cenfit(beach_a$observed, beach_a$censored)

# Print summary statistics estimated from KM
print(km_a)
##        n    n.cen   median     mean       sd 
## 24.00000  0.00000 19.83262 31.09971 28.21992
# Plot the KM CDF
par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 3.5, 2), las = 1,
    col.axis = "#3a3a38", col.lab = "#1a1a18", cex.axis = 0.9)

plot(km_a,
     xlab = "E. coli (CFU/100 mL)",
     ylab = "Cumulative probability",
     main = "Kaplan–Meier CDF — E. coli Beach A",
     col  = "#4a7c5e", lwd = 2)

# Mark the standard
abline(v = 235, lty = 2, col = "#c8832a", lwd = 1.8)
text(250, 0.15, "235 CFU/100 mL\n(state standard)", col = "#c8832a",
     adj = 0, cex = 0.82)

# Mark the median
med_a <- median(km_a)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 3, col = "#c62828", lwd = 1.4)
abline(v = med_a, lty = 3, col = "#c62828", lwd = 1.4)
text(med_a + 5, 0.05, paste0("Median ≈ ", round(med_a, 1)), col = "#c62828",
     adj = 0, cex = 0.80)

Kaplan–Meier empirical CDF for E. coli concentrations at Beach A. The shaded step function drops at each detected value; the flat segments between detection limits are where non-detects contribute. The red dashed line marks the 50th percentile (median). The dashed vertical line marks the state standard of 235 CFU/100 mL.

Comparing three beach sites with KM

One of KM’s great strengths is comparing groups without any distributional assumption. We fit separate KM curves and then apply the non-parametric log-rank-type test (cendiff()) for equality of the distributions.

km_all <- cenfit(ecoli$observed, ecoli$censored, groups = factor(ecoli$site))

par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 3.5, 2), las = 1)
plot(km_all,
     xlab = "E. coli (CFU/100 mL)",
     ylab = "Cumulative probability",
     main = "Kaplan–Meier CDF — E. coli by Site",
     col  = c("#1e3a2f", "#4a7c5e", "#c8832a"), lwd = 2)
abline(v = 235, lty = 2, col = "#c62828", lwd = 1.5)
abline(h = 0.50, lty = 3, col = "#999", lwd = 1)
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Beach A", "Beach B", "Beach C", "235 CFU standard"),
       col    = c("#1e3a2f", "#4a7c5e", "#c8832a", "#c62828"),
       lty    = c(1, 1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

Kaplan–Meier CDFs for E. coli at three beach sites. The curves are well separated: Beach C (high E. coli) stacks far right, Beach B is intermediate, and Beach A has the lowest concentrations. The horizontal dashed line at p = 0.50 reads off each median; the vertical line marks the 235 CFU/100 mL standard. 

# Non-parametric test for equality of distributions across sites
cendiff(ecoli$observed, ecoli$censored, groups = factor(ecoli$site))
##                             N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
## factor(ecoli$site)=Beach A 24     11.0    13.29     0.381     0.895
## factor(ecoli$site)=Beach B 24      7.9    16.35     4.362    12.157
## factor(ecoli$site)=Beach C 24     17.5     6.82    16.771    28.499
## 
##  Chisq= 30.2  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 3e-07

📌 Reading the output of cendiff()

cendiff() performs a Peto–Peto modified log-rank test adapted for left-censored data. The test statistic and p-value test H₀: all groups have the same distribution. A small p-value (< 0.05) tells you the distributions differ significantly — it does not tell you which pairs differ. For pairwise comparisons, use cenperm2() from NADA2 (see Section 8).

6. Regression on Order Statistics (ROS)

Regression on Order Statistics (ROS) is a semi-parametric method that estimates summary statistics by:

  1. Ranking all observations together (detected and non-detected).
  2. Computing expected normal (or log-normal) scores for the detected values.
  3. Fitting a regression of detected values on their normal scores.
  4. Extrapolating that regression line to predict what the non-detected values would have been, then substituting those modeled values.

The result is a complete dataset of modeled values that you can summarise or plot like ordinary data, as long as you remember that the non-detect slots have been imputed, not measured.

Fitting ROS for phosphorus

# ROS fit for total phosphorus — surface station
surf_tp <- tp |> filter(depth == "Surface")

ros_tp <- cenros(surf_tp$observed, surf_tp$censored)

# The returned object has $modeled — the full imputed dataset
cat("ROS-estimated mean TP (surface):", round(mean(ros_tp$modeled), 2), "µg/L\n")
## ROS-estimated mean TP (surface): 13.37 µg/L
cat("ROS-estimated SD   TP (surface):", round(sd(ros_tp$modeled),   2), "µg/L\n")
## ROS-estimated SD   TP (surface): 14.41 µg/L
cat("95th percentile (surface):       ", round(quantile(ros_tp$modeled, 0.95), 2), "µg/L\n")
## 95th percentile (surface):        35.77 µg/L
par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 3.5, 2), las = 1)

# cenros() $modeled contains the full imputed dataset (NDs replaced by fitted values).
# We compute z-scores from Blom plotting positions on the complete modeled vector
# rather than using $zscores, which can contain NAs when many values are censored.
n_all      <- length(ros_tp$modeled)
pp         <- (rank(ros_tp$modeled) - 0.375) / (n_all + 0.25)
z_all      <- qnorm(pp)

is_det     <- !ros_tp$censored
x_detected <- ros_tp$modeled[is_det]
y_detected <- z_all[is_det]
x_modeled  <- ros_tp$modeled[!is_det]
y_modeled  <- z_all[!is_det]

# Compute safe axis limits (finite values only)
x_rng <- range(c(x_detected, x_modeled), finite = TRUE)
y_rng <- range(c(y_detected, y_modeled), finite = TRUE)
x_rng <- x_rng + c(-0.05, 0.05) * diff(x_rng)
y_rng <- y_rng + c(-0.05, 0.05) * diff(y_rng)

plot(x_detected, y_detected,
     pch = 19, col = "#4a7c5e", cex = 1.1,
     xlab = "Total phosphorus (µg/L)",
     ylab = "Normal score (z)",
     main = "ROS Probability Plot — Total Phosphorus (Surface)",
     xlim = x_rng, ylim = y_rng)

if (length(x_modeled) > 0)
  points(x_modeled, y_modeled, pch = 1, col = "#c62828", cex = 1.2, lwd = 1.5)

abline(v = surf_tp$rl[1], lty = 2, col = "#999", lwd = 1.5)
text(surf_tp$rl[1] + diff(x_rng) * 0.02, y_rng[1] + diff(y_rng) * 0.05,
     "RL = 5 µg/L", col = "#777", adj = 0, cex = 0.80)
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Detected values", "ROS-modeled (imputed)"),
       pch    = c(19, 1),
       col    = c("#4a7c5e", "#c62828"),
       bty    = "n", cex = 0.88)

Probability plot for total phosphorus (surface samples) from the ROS fit. Blue circles are detected values; open red circles are the modeled (imputed) values extrapolated below the reporting limit (grey dashed vertical line). The modeled values extend the linear trend established by the detected values into the censored region.

Comparing surface and deep TP with ROS

deep_tp  <- tp |> filter(depth == "Deep")
ros_deep <- cenros(deep_tp$observed, deep_tp$censored)

ros_summary <- data.frame(
  Depth    = c("Surface", "Deep"),
  n        = c(nrow(surf_tp), nrow(deep_tp)),
  pct_nd   = round(c(mean(surf_tp$censored), mean(deep_tp$censored)) * 100, 1),
  mean_ros = round(c(mean(ros_tp$modeled), mean(ros_deep$modeled)), 2),
  sd_ros   = round(c(sd(ros_tp$modeled),   sd(ros_deep$modeled)),   2),
  p95_ros  = round(c(quantile(ros_tp$modeled, 0.95),
                     quantile(ros_deep$modeled, 0.95)), 2)
)

kable(ros_summary,
      col.names = c("Depth", "n", "% ND", "Mean (µg/L)", "SD", "95th pct"),
      caption   = "ROS-estimated total phosphorus statistics by depth stratum.")
ROS-estimated total phosphorus statistics by depth stratum.
Depth n % ND Mean (µg/L) SD 95th pct
Surface 30 23.3 13.37 14.41 35.77
Deep 30 3.3 24.32 18.08 59.84

7. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

Maximum Likelihood Estimation fits a parametric distribution (usually log-normal) to the observed data, explicitly accounting for censoring in the likelihood function. Each detected value contributes the density f(x); each non-detect at RL contributes the probability F(RL) — the probability that the true value fell below the detection limit.

The log-likelihood for a log-normal distribution with n detected values and m non-detects is:

\[\ell(\mu, \sigma) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(x_i;\, \mu, \sigma) \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{m} \log F(RL_j;\, \mu, \sigma)\]

Maximising this over (µ, σ) gives the MLE of the log-normal parameters, from which means, percentiles, and confidence intervals follow analytically.

MLE for lead (Pb) in drinking water

# cenmle() / survreg() require strictly positive values even for non-detects.
# Non-detects are coded as 0 in pb$observed; replace with the RL so that
# survreg sees a valid left-censored value (the true value is known to be < RL).
pb_obs_mle <- ifelse(pb$censored, pb$rl, pb$observed)

mle_pb <- cenmle(pb_obs_mle, pb$censored, dist = "lognormal")
print(mle_pb)
##         n     n.cen    median      mean        sd 
## 50.000000  6.000000  2.290607  5.489231 11.954398
# Extract mean and confidence interval
mle_stats <- summary(mle_pb)
cat("MLE log-normal fit for Pb:\n")
## MLE log-normal fit for Pb:
cat("  Mean:     ", round(mean(mle_pb),  3), "µg/L\n")
##   Mean:      5.489 1.691 3.332 9.044 µg/L
cat("  Median:   ", round(median(mle_pb),3), "µg/L\n")
##   Median:    2.291 µg/L
cat("  95th pct: ", round(quantile(mle_pb, p = 0.95), 3), "µg/L\n")
##   95th pct:  20.155 µg/L

Checking the distributional assumption with a Q–Q plot

MLE depends on the assumed distribution being correct. Always check with a Q–Q plot.

par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 3.5, 2), las = 1)
cenQQ(pb_obs_mle, pb$censored)
title(main = "Log-normal Q–Q Plot — Lead (Pb)", cex.main = 0.95)

Censored Q–Q plot for lead (Pb) concentrations. Detected values (filled circles) are plotted against log-normal quantiles; a good fit follows the diagonal reference line. Non-detects are shown at the reporting limit boundary (0.5 µg/L).

When MLE is preferred over ROS

Method comparison for handling non-detects.
Criterion Kaplan–Meier ROS MLE
Distributional assumption None Log-normal (soft) Log-normal (strict)
Handles multiple RLs Yes Yes Yes
Censoring fraction Any < 80% Any
Provides CIs Bootstrap only Bootstrap Analytical
Easy to visualise Yes (CDF) Yes (prob plot) Moderate
Sensitive to outliers Low Moderate Moderate

8. Putting It Together: PM2.5 Analysis

The PM2.5 dataset combines seasonal structure, a meaningful detection limit, and a regulatory threshold. We walk through the complete analysis workflow.

Step 1 — Visualise the raw data

pm25_plot <- pm25 |>
  mutate(season = factor(season, levels = c("Winter","Spring","Summer","Fall")))

ggplot(pm25_plot, aes(x = doy, y = observed)) +
  geom_point(data = filter(pm25_plot, !censored),
             aes(colour = season), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = filter(pm25_plot, censored),
             shape = 25, colour = "#c62828", fill = "#c62828",
             size = 1.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 35, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c8832a", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = 37, label = "35 µg/m³ NAAQS", colour = "#c8832a",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1e3a2f","#4a7c5e","#c8832a","#8aad96"),
                      name = "Season") +
  labs(x = "Day of year", y = expression(PM[2.5]~(µg/m^3)),
       title = expression(Daily~PM[2.5]~concentrations~(rural~background~site))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_text(family = "serif", face = "bold", colour = "#1e3a2f"))

Daily PM2.5 concentrations over one year. Grey points are detected values; red triangles pointing down indicate non-detect days (coded as 0 in the raw data). The 35 µg/m³ NAAQS is shown as a dashed horizontal line. Non-detects cluster in summer, when clean-air conditions are most frequent.

Step 2 — Fit KM and compute seasonal summary statistics

# Compute KM-estimated mean and median by season
seasons <- c("Winter","Spring","Summer","Fall")

pm25_stats <- lapply(seasons, function(s) {
  d       <- filter(pm25, season == s)
  # Replace 0 (non-detect) with RL for cenmle; KM/cenfit handle 0s natively
  obs_mle <- ifelse(d$censored, d$rl, d$observed)
  km  <- cenfit(d$observed, d$censored)
  mle <- tryCatch(cenmle(obs_mle, d$censored, dist = "lognormal"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
  data.frame(
    Season   = s,
    n        = nrow(d),
    pct_nd   = round(100 * mean(d$censored), 1),
    km_mean  = round(mean(km),   2),
    km_med   = round(median(km), 2),
    mle_mean = if (!is.null(mle)) round(mean(mle),   2) else NA
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

kable(pm25_stats,
      col.names = c("Season", "n", "% ND", "KM mean", "KM median", "MLE mean"),
      caption   = "PM2.5 seasonal summary statistics (µg/m³) from Kaplan–Meier and MLE fits.")

# Peto-Peto test across seasons
cendiff(pm25$observed, pm25$censored, groups = factor(pm25$season))
##                             N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
## factor(pm25$season)=Winter 89     57.5     31.0     22.69     38.41
## factor(pm25$season)=Spring 92     41.0     48.6      1.18      2.37
## factor(pm25$season)=Summer 92     26.5     60.5     19.05     44.49
## factor(pm25$season)=Fall   92     53.1     38.1      5.89     10.63

Step 4 — Exceedance probability

What fraction of days exceed the 35 µg/m³ NAAQS? Because detected values > 35 are always detects, we can compute this directly from the detected data.

exceed_stats <- pm25 |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    n_days       = n(),
    n_exceed     = sum(observed > 35, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_exceed   = round(100 * mean(observed > 35, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    annual_frac  = round(n_exceed / 365 * 100, 1)
  )

kable(exceed_stats,
      col.names = c("Season", "Days", "Exceedances", "% of season", "% of year"),
      caption   = "PM2.5 exceedances of the 35 µg/m³ 24-hour NAAQS by season.")

9. Hypothesis Tests for Censored Data

Standard t-tests and ANOVA are invalid when a substantial fraction of observations are non-detects. The NADA2 package provides censored analogues.

Two-sample test: Lead levels in older vs. newer homes

# Simulate: older homes (pre-1978) have higher Pb than newer homes
set.seed(505)
pb2 <- bind_rows(
  sim_censored(30, meanlog = 1.5, sdlog = 1.2, rl = 0.5) |>
    mutate(era = "Pre-1978"),
  sim_censored(30, meanlog = 0.3, sdlog = 1.1, rl = 0.5) |>
    mutate(era = "Post-1978")
)

cat("Pre-1978 non-detects: ", sum(pb2$censored[pb2$era == "Pre-1978"]),
    "/30 (", round(100*mean(pb2$censored[pb2$era == "Pre-1978"]),1),"%)\n")
## Pre-1978 non-detects:  3 /30 ( 10 %)
cat("Post-1978 non-detects:", sum(pb2$censored[pb2$era == "Post-1978"]),
    "/30 (", round(100*mean(pb2$censored[pb2$era == "Post-1978"]),1),"%)\n\n")
## Post-1978 non-detects: 7 /30 ( 23.3 %)
# Censored Wilcoxon / Score test via cendiff()
cendiff(pb2$observed, pb2$censored, groups = factor(pb2$era))
##                            N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
## factor(pb2$era)=Post-1978 30     10.3     18.9      3.87      15.5
## factor(pb2$era)=Pre-1978  30     19.2     10.7      6.83      15.5
## 
##  Chisq= 15.5  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 8e-05

Pairwise comparisons for E. coli across sites

When comparing more than two groups, use cenperm2() from NADA2 for permutation-based pairwise tests with multiple comparison adjustment.

# Permutation-based pairwise test (BH adjustment by default)
cenperm2(ecoli$observed, ecoli$censored, factor(ecoli$site))
##  Permutation test of mean CensData: ecoli$observed   by Factor: factor(ecoli$site) 
##      9999 Permutations     alternative = two.sided 
##   mean of Beach A = 31.1 to 31.1     mean of Beach B = 17.75 to 17.75 
##      Mean (Beach A - Beach B) =  13.35 to 13.35       p = 0.3687 to 0.3687 
##

Correlation with censored data

Does phosphorus increase with turbidity? Standard Pearson r is biased when either variable contains non-detects. Use Kendall’s τ via cenken().

set.seed(606)
# Simulate turbidity (NTU) — positively correlated with TP, no non-detects
n_corr <- 40
turb_ntu <- rexp(n_corr, rate = 0.08) + 2

# TP correlated with turbidity, with non-detects
tp_corr <- 3 + 1.2 * turb_ntu + rnorm(n_corr, 0, 4)
obs_tp  <- pmax(tp_corr, 0)
nd_tp   <- tp_corr < 5
obs_tp[nd_tp] <- 0

# Kendall's tau for censored data
cenken(obs_tp, nd_tp, turb_ntu)
## Censored Kendall's Tau Regression:
## Slope     : 1.20433 
## Intercept : 3.907174 
## Tau       : 0.7717949 
## p-value   : 2.420508e-12

📌 Censored Kendall’s τ

cenken() computes Akritas–Murphy–LaValley (AML) Kendall’s τ, a rank-based correlation coefficient that discards or downweights pairs where at least one member is a non-detect. The test is valid as long as the censoring fraction is below ~70–80%. The sign and magnitude of τ are interpreted exactly like ordinary Kendall’s τ: positive means the two variables tend to increase together.

10. Reporting Non-Detect Statistics

What to always report

Reporting non-detects transparently is both a scientific and a regulatory obligation. Every summary table of censored data should include:

  1. Sample size (total n)
  2. Number and fraction of non-detects (e.g., “12/40, 30%”)
  3. Reporting limit(s) (and whether multiple RLs were present)
  4. The method used (KM, ROS, MLE, substitution) with a citation
  5. Estimates with uncertainty (mean ± SE or 95% CI; percentiles)

Complete example: Water quality summary table

# Compute KM statistics for all four contaminants in a unified format
datasets <- list(
  "E. coli (Beach A, CFU/100 mL)" = list(obs = beach_a$observed,
                                           cen = beach_a$censored, rl = 1),
  "E. coli (Beach C, CFU/100 mL)" = list(obs = filter(ecoli, site=="Beach C")$observed,
                                           cen = filter(ecoli, site=="Beach C")$censored, rl = 1),
  "Total P – Surface (µg/L)"      = list(obs = surf_tp$observed,
                                           cen = surf_tp$censored, rl = 5),
  "Lead Pb (µg/L)"                = list(obs = pb$observed,
                                           cen = pb$censored, rl = 0.5),
  "PM2.5 – Winter (µg/m³)"        = list(obs = filter(pm25, season=="Winter")$observed,
                                           cen = filter(pm25, season=="Winter")$censored, rl = 2)
)

final_tbl <- lapply(names(datasets), function(nm) {
  d  <- datasets[[nm]]
  km <- cenfit(d$obs, d$cen)
  data.frame(
    Contaminant = nm,
    n           = length(d$obs),
    ND          = paste0(sum(d$cen), " (", round(100*mean(d$cen),0), "%)"),
    RL          = d$rl,
    KM_mean     = round(mean(km), 2),
    KM_median   = round(median(km), 2),
    Method      = "Kaplan–Meier"
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

kable(final_tbl,
      col.names = c("Contaminant (units)", "n", "Non-detects",
                    "RL", "Mean", "Median", "Method"),
      caption   = "Summary statistics for environmental monitoring data with non-detects. All estimates are from Kaplan–Meier using the NADA package (Helsel et al. 2020).") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped")

Common mistakes checklist

Mistake 1
“I replaced all non-detects with zero because the instrument read zero.”
Correct approach: Zero on a lab report means below the reporting limit, not truly zero. Use cenfit() or cenros(). Even 15% non-detects can meaningfully bias a mean when substituting zero.
Mistake 2
“I dropped all non-detects from the dataset to avoid the problem.”
Correct approach: Deleting non-detects removes the cleanest observations. Summary statistics will be biased high and you lose power. Every data point — detected or not — belongs in the analysis.
Mistake 3
“I used RL/2 substitution; my professor said that’s acceptable.”
Correct approach: RL/2 is acceptable only when the censoring fraction is below ~15% and the distribution is approximately log-normal. Above 15–20% non-detects, bias increases rapidly. Use ROS or MLE instead.
Mistake 4
“I ran a t-test on the data after RL/2 substitution.”
Correct approach: Substituted data are not ordinary continuous data — the t-test’s distributional assumptions are violated. Use cendiff() for two-group comparisons or cenperm2() for multiple groups.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Non-detects are left-censored observations, not zeros and not missing data. A result of “< RL” carries real information: the true value lies in [0, RL].
  • Substitution methods (0, RL/2, RL) are biased whenever the censoring fraction exceeds ~15%. The bias is systematic and worsens with higher censoring.
  • Kaplan–Meier (cenfit()) is non-parametric, handles multiple reporting limits, and is the safest choice when you cannot verify distributional assumptions. It is the baseline method.
  • ROS (cenros()) produces a complete imputed dataset useful for visualization and regression; valid up to ~80% censoring when data are approximately log-normal.
  • MLE (cenmle()) gives analytical confidence intervals and is most efficient when the distributional assumption is correct. Check with a censored Q–Q plot (cenQQ()).
  • Use cendiff() for group comparisons and cenken() for censored correlations. Never apply standard t-tests or ANOVA directly to substituted data.
  • Always report: n, number and fraction of non-detects, the reporting limit, and the method used — with a citation to Helsel (2012).

What’s next?

  • Survival Analysis — the right-censored twin of this problem; time-to-event methods with the same KM and Cox machinery
  • Time Series — detecting trends in long-term monitoring data that also contain non-detects (Mann–Kendall with censoring)
  • Multiple Regression & GLMs — building predictive models when the response variable contains non-detects

Further reading

  • Helsel, D.R. (2012). Statistics for Censored Environmental Data Using Minitab and R, 2nd ed. Wiley. — The authoritative reference; all methods here follow Helsel’s framework.
  • Helsel, D.R., Hirsch, R.M., et al. (2020). Statistical Methods in Water Resources, USGS Techniques and Methods 4–A3. Freely available at pubs.usgs.gov.
  • USEPA (2009). Statistical Analysis of Groundwater Monitoring Data at RCRA Facilities: Unified Guidance. EPA 530/R-09-007. — regulatory context for non-detect handling.
